families.name: Swarm intelligence
families.description: Population methods driven by distributed social information and collective motion.

families.name: Evolutionary methods
families.description: Population methods based on stochastic variation, recombination, selection and adaptive control parameters.

families.name: Trajectory-based methods
families.description: Single-solution methods that explore a neighborhood trajectory through explicit acceptance and state-transition policies.

families.name: Hybrid / memetic methods
families.description: Compositions of population, trajectory, local-search, decoder and exact/heuristic subsolver mechanisms.

families.name: Constructive methods
families.description: Methods that build complete solutions progressively from domain-defined components, often followed by local improvement.

algorithms.name: Particle Swarm Optimization
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration for the canonical graphless fast path; topology/social policies may add overhead
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces; generic platform infrastructure also supports alternative social/topology policies
algorithms.publication: Kennedy & Eberhart (1995), Particle Swarm Optimization, IEEE ICNN; Clerc & Kennedy (2002), The particle swarm — explosion, stability, and convergence in a multidimensional complex space, IEEE TEC 6(1), 58–73
algorithms.implementation: Flat particle-major buffers, deterministic target-owned RNG streams, graphless fully-connected canonical fast path, calibrated movement/evaluation parallelism.
algorithms.assumptions: The canonical implementation assumes a bounded continuous representation. Stability results depend on the chosen inertia/constriction and stochastic assumptions; topology changes the social guide but not the generic state model.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made. Under the Clerc–Kennedy constriction analysis, stability conditions can be derived for the linearized stochastic dynamics; practical convergence still depends on objective, topology and parameterization.

algorithms.name: Differential Evolution
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation for classical mutation/crossover, plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces
algorithms.publication: Storn & Price (1997), Differential Evolution — A Simple and Efficient Heuristic for Global Optimization over Continuous Spaces, Journal of Global Optimization 11(4), 341–359
algorithms.implementation: Flat parent/trial buffers; classical mutation and crossover strategies; deterministic per-target RNG; calibrated variation and independent evaluation parallelism.
algorithms.assumptions: A population of distinct donor indices is required; the represented domain is continuous and bounded by the configured boundary policy.
algorithms.convergence: The implementation does not claim a general deterministic convergence rate. DE is stochastic; convergence analyses require additional assumptions on mutation, selection and persistent exploration.

algorithms.name: jDE — Self-Adaptive Differential Evolution
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces; canonical DE/rand/1/bin self-adaptation
algorithms.publication: Brest et al. (2006), Self-Adapting Control Parameters in Differential Evolution: A Comparative Study on Numerical Benchmark Problems, IEEE TEC 10(6), 646–657
algorithms.implementation: Per-individual inherited F_i/CR_i proposals; trial parameters are committed only after strict successful selection.
algorithms.assumptions: Canonical DE/rand/1/bin donor feasibility and a continuous bounded decision vector.
algorithms.convergence: Self-adaptation changes the stochastic parameter process but does not introduce a universal finite-time convergence guarantee.

algorithms.name: JADE
algorithms.time: O(ND + N log N) per generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.space: O(ND) population plus O(ND) optional archive
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces
algorithms.publication: Zhang & Sanderson (2009), JADE: Adaptive Differential Evolution With Optional External Archive, IEEE TEC 13(5), 945–958
algorithms.implementation: current-to-pbest/1/bin, optional external archive, Cauchy F sampling, normal CR sampling and success-mean adaptation.
algorithms.assumptions: Continuous bounded domain; p-best ranking is defined from current objective values; archive ownership is explicit.
algorithms.convergence: JADE is an adaptive stochastic heuristic; no universal rate is asserted by the library.

algorithms.name: SHADE
algorithms.time: O(ND + N log N) per generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces
algorithms.publication: Tanabe & Fukunaga (2013), Success-History Based Parameter Adaptation for Differential Evolution, IEEE CEC, 71–78
algorithms.implementation: Historical memories M_F/M_CR, random memory slot per target, improvement-weighted success learning and external archive.
algorithms.assumptions: Strict improvements define the success set; no-success generations leave historical memory unchanged.
algorithms.convergence: SHADE adapts sampling distributions from successful history but does not supply a universal deterministic convergence rate.

algorithms.name: L-SHADE
algorithms.time: O(N_kD + N_k log N_k) at generation k plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces with an evaluation budget driving LPSR
algorithms.publication: Tanabe & Fukunaga (2014), Improving the Search Performance of SHADE Using Linear Population Size Reduction, IEEE CEC, 1658–1665
algorithms.implementation: SHADE 1.1 success-history semantics with linear population-size reduction, fixed physical capacity and shrinking active prefix.
algorithms.assumptions: An explicit evaluation budget defines the population-reduction schedule; the active population never falls below four.
algorithms.convergence: LPSR is a resource-allocation mechanism layered on SHADE; the implementation makes no universal finite-time convergence claim.

algorithms.name: Simulated Annealing
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact differential evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); no mandatory per-transition solution clone on the reversible path
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Metropolis et al. (1953), Journal of Chemical Physics 21(6), 1087–1092; Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983), Science 220(4598), 671–680
algorithms.implementation: Generic reversible trajectory engine, Metropolis acceptance, ten built-in scientific cooling laws plus custom schedules, allocation-free statistical-cooling fast path, exact-delta fast path and common OptimizationContext lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: The neighborhood must be sampleable and moves must be reversible for the zero-clone fast path. Cooling schedule assumptions depend on the chosen schedule.
algorithms.convergence: Classical asymptotic global-convergence theorems require sufficiently slow logarithmic cooling under irreducibility/communication assumptions. The practical geometric default does not claim that theorem.

algorithms.name: Tabu Search
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)| * C_delta + log M) per iteration with exact deltas; otherwise O(|N(x)| * (C_move + C_eval + C_undo) + log M)
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + M) for retained short-term tabu records
algorithms.applicability: Any finite enumerated neighborhood with reversible moves and domain-defined tabu attributes
algorithms.publication: Glover (1989), Tabu Search-Part I, ORSA Journal on Computing 1(3), 190-206; Glover (1990), Tabu Search-Part II, ORSA Journal on Computing 2(1), 4-32
algorithms.implementation: Allocation-free best-admissible neighborhood scan, attribute-based expiration memory, best-so-far aspiration, fixed or varying tenure, exact-delta fast path and reversible full-evaluation fallback.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite neighborhood enumeration, stable tabu-attribute equality/hash semantics, and exactness of any supplied delta evaluator. The attribute mapping defines which reversals or features are forbidden.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global-optimum guarantee is claimed. Classical behavior depends on neighborhood, attribute memory, tenure, aspiration and optional longer-term strategies.

algorithms.name: Reactive Tabu Search
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)| * C_delta + log M_s) per normal iteration with exact deltas; escape steps reservoir-scan N(x) and evaluate one selected move
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + M_s + M_f + M_r) for short-term, frequency and repetition memories
algorithms.applicability: Finite enumerated neighborhoods with reversible moves, domain-defined tabu attributes and a stable configuration signature
algorithms.publication: Battiti & Tecchiolli (1994), The Reactive Tabu Search, ORSA Journal on Computing 6(2), 126-140; Glover (1989, 1990)
algorithms.implementation: Explicit repetition detection, feedback tabu tenure, cycle-length moving average, reactive random-walk escape, optional frequency diversification, optional elite intensification, exact-delta fast path and common OptimizationContext lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite neighborhood enumeration, stable tabu-attribute semantics, stable domain-owned configuration signatures, and exactness of any supplied delta evaluator.
algorithms.convergence: Reactive Tabu Search is an adaptive memory-based heuristic; no universal finite-time global-optimum guarantee is claimed.

algorithms.name: Local Search — Best Improvement
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)| C_delta) per descent step with exact deltas; reversible full evaluation otherwise
algorithms.applicability: Finite enumerated neighborhoods with reversible moves
algorithms.publication: Talbi (2009), Metaheuristics: From Design to Implementation
algorithms.implementation: Steepest-descent best-improvement scan with allocation-free neighborhood cursor, exact-delta fast path and reversible fallback.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite neighborhood; exact delta evaluator, when supplied, must match full objective evaluation.
algorithms.convergence: Terminates at a local optimum under finite neighborhoods and strict improvement, absent earlier generic stopping.

algorithms.name: Local Search — First Improvement
algorithms.time: O(q C_delta) per accepted move, where q is the number of candidates scanned until first improvement
algorithms.applicability: Finite ordered neighborhoods with reversible moves
algorithms.publication: Talbi (2009), Metaheuristics: From Design to Implementation
algorithms.implementation: First-descent scan that stops immediately at the first strict improving move.
algorithms.assumptions: Neighborhood enumeration order is meaningful; strict improvement prevents objective cycles.
algorithms.convergence: Terminates at an order-dependent local optimum for finite neighborhoods under strict improvement.

algorithms.name: Multi-Start Local Search
algorithms.time: O(S * (C_init + C_LS)) for S starts; C_LS depends on the composed local search
algorithms.applicability: Any representation with an initial-solution generator and a reusable compatible local-search procedure
algorithms.publication: Marti (2003), Multi-Start Methods, Handbook of Metaheuristics, pp. 355-368
algorithms.implementation: Sequential independent starts composed with the reusable v0.23 local-search procedure and one common OptimizationContext.
algorithms.assumptions: The generator returns valid starts and the composed local search respects the common procedure contract; probabilistic independence is not assumed unless supplied by the generator.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-start guarantee; under independent starts with fixed positive probability p of entering a globally optimal basin, failure probability is (1-p)^S and tends to zero.

algorithms.name: Iterated Local Search - Lourenco-Martin-Stutzle
algorithms.time: O(C_LS0 + sum_k(C_perturb,k + C_eval,k + C_LS,k))
algorithms.applicability: Representations admitting a reusable local search, owned cloning and a domain-defined perturbation
algorithms.publication: Lourenco, Martin & Stutzle (2003), Iterated Local Search, Handbook of Metaheuristics, pp. 320-353
algorithms.implementation: Canonical initial local search, perturbation, local search and acceptance framework; global best is independent from incumbent acceptance.
algorithms.assumptions: Perturbation produces evaluable candidates; cloning owns candidate state; useful basin transitions depend on the domain perturbation/local-search pair.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim; asymptotic results require additional reachability or ergodicity and acceptance assumptions.

algorithms.name: Variable Neighborhood Descent
algorithms.time: O(sum_k C_LS,k) per non-improving sweep, with restart after every strict improvement
algorithms.applicability: Any representation with an ordered set of compatible reusable local-search neighborhoods
algorithms.publication: Mladenovic & Hansen (1997), Variable neighborhood search; Hansen & Mladenovic (2001), Variable neighborhood search: Principles and applications
algorithms.implementation: Reusable ordered VND over ILocalSearchProcedure<TSolution>; strict improvement resets to the first neighborhood.
algorithms.assumptions: All local-search procedures operate on one representation and objective; strict improvement is defined by the problem optimization sense.
algorithms.convergence: On finite spaces with strictly improving transitions, VND terminates at a solution locally optimal for every configured neighborhood unless externally stopped.

algorithms.name: Variable Neighborhood Search - Mladenovic-Hansen
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval + C_LS)) per complete non-improving shaking sweep
algorithms.applicability: Any representation with ordered shaking neighborhoods and a compatible reusable local-search procedure
algorithms.publication: Mladenovic & Hansen (1997), Variable neighborhood search; Hansen & Mladenovic (2001), Variable neighborhood search: Principles and applications
algorithms.implementation: Canonical basic VNS with ordered shaking, local improvement, strict incumbent acceptance and restart at the first shaking neighborhood.
algorithms.assumptions: Each shaking operator and local search are valid for the same solution representation; useful basin reachability depends on the domain neighborhood system.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence theorem is claimed; asymptotic reachability requires additional domain-specific stochastic assumptions.

algorithms.name: Guided Local Search - Voudouris-Tsang
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)|*(C_delta_f+C_delta_p)) per guided scan on the exact-delta fast path; reversible full evaluation and active-feature scans otherwise
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + P) for P distinct penalized features
algorithms.applicability: Reversible move neighborhoods plus domain-defined unique active features with finite non-negative feature costs
algorithms.publication: Tsang & Voudouris (1997), Fast local search and guided local search; Voudouris & Tsang (1999), Guided local search and its application to the traveling salesman problem
algorithms.implementation: Canonical augmented-objective GLS with feature-utility penalties, exact objective-delta and penalty-sum-delta fast paths, and original-objective best-so-far ownership.
algorithms.assumptions: Active features are unique per solution; feature costs are finite and non-negative; optional delta evaluators are exact.
algorithms.convergence: Each strict augmented-descent phase terminates on finite spaces for fixed penalties; the finite penalty-update cap guarantees library termination, without a universal global-optimum guarantee.

algorithms.name: Reduced Variable Neighborhood Search
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval,k)) per complete non-improving shaking sweep
algorithms.applicability: Ordered shaking neighborhoods; useful when repeated local search is too expensive
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Mladenovic (2001); Hansen, Mladenovic, Todosijevic & Hanafi (2017)
algorithms.implementation: Canonical RVNS omitting the local-improvement phase while preserving VNS shaking and neighborhood change.
algorithms.assumptions: Ordered shaking neighborhoods generate valid candidates.
algorithms.convergence: Finite MaximumCycles guarantees termination; no universal global-optimum guarantee.

algorithms.name: General Variable Neighborhood Search
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval,k + C_VND,k)) per complete non-improving shaking sweep
algorithms.applicability: Ordered shaking neighborhoods and compatible reusable VND local-search neighborhoods
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Mladenovic (2001); Hansen, Mladenovic, Todosijevic & Hanafi (2017)
algorithms.implementation: Canonical GVNS using the existing VariableNeighborhoodDescentProcedure as its improvement phase.
algorithms.assumptions: Shaking and all VND neighborhoods operate on the same solution representation.
algorithms.convergence: Finite VND safety caps and MaximumCycles guarantee termination.

algorithms.name: Skewed Variable Neighborhood Search - Hansen-Mladenovic
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval,k + C_LS,k + C_distance,k)) per complete non-accepting sweep
algorithms.applicability: Shaking, reusable local search and a finite non-negative domain distance
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Mladenovic (2001), Variable neighborhood search: Principles and applications; Hansen et al. (2017)
algorithms.implementation: Canonical distance-skewed recentering with sense-consistent minimization/maximization handling and independent original-objective best-so-far.
algorithms.assumptions: Distance is finite and non-negative; local search and shaking return valid candidates.
algorithms.convergence: Finite MaximumCycles guarantees termination; skewed recentering has no universal global-optimum guarantee.

algorithms.name: GRASP - Feo-Resende
algorithms.time: O(2 * sum_t |C_t| * C_g + C_eval + C_LS) per outer iteration
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + construction cursor + local-search workspace); RCL overhead O(1)
algorithms.applicability: Constructive problems with domain-defined finite greedy scores, restartable candidate cursors and compatible local search
algorithms.publication: Feo & Resende (1989), A probabilistic heuristic for a computationally difficult set covering problem; Feo & Resende (1995), Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures
algorithms.implementation: Canonical adaptive threshold-RCL construction; two allocation-free candidate scans; uniform reservoir sampling; reusable local search; common OptimizationContext.
algorithms.update:
\begin{aligned}
c_{\min}&=\min_{e\in C}c(e),\qquad
c_{\max}=\max_{e\in C}c(e),\\
\tau_\alpha&=c_{\min}+\alpha(c_{\max}-c_{\min}),\\
RCL_\alpha&=\{e\in C:c(e)\le\tau_\alpha\},\\
x'&=LS(x)
\end{aligned}
algorithms.assumptions: The domain supplies a complete constructive model with finite side-effect-free greedy scores, restartable candidate cursors and a compatible local search.
algorithms.convergence: No unconditional finite-time global convergence claim; with positive probability of reaching a globally optimal basin and indefinitely many independent iterations, failure probability tends to zero.

algorithms.name: Reactive GRASP - Prais-Ribeiro
algorithms.time: Canonical GRASP construction/local-search cost plus O(m) alpha sampling and periodic O(m) probability updates
algorithms.space: Canonical GRASP workspace plus O(m) reactive alpha statistics
algorithms.applicability: Constructive problems with strictly positive objective values, reusable GRASP construction and compatible local search
algorithms.publication: Prais & Ribeiro (2000), Reactive GRASP: An Application to a Matrix Decomposition Problem in TDMA Traffic Assignment
algorithms.implementation: Per-run discrete alpha controller, uniform initial probabilities, online per-alpha means, periodic Prais-Ribeiro ratio updates, canonical GRASP construction and common lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: Configured alpha values are finite and unique in [0,1]; the canonical ratio update requires strictly positive objective observations.
algorithms.convergence: No unconditional finite-time global convergence claim; adaptive alpha probabilities preserve stochastic sampling while useful alpha values retain positive probability.

algorithms.name: GRASP with Path Relinking
algorithms.time: Canonical GRASP + online pairwise PR; optional EvPR adds O(E^2*C_PR) per evolutionary generation plus optional offspring local-search cost.
algorithms.space: O(E*|solution| + path workspace) online; EvPR keeps bounded current/next elite populations, still O(E*|solution|), plus O(P_k) pooled randomized-path probes.
algorithms.applicability: Finite attribute-based path spaces with GRASP construction, compatible local search, non-negative integral distance and target-directed reversible moves
algorithms.publication: Resende & Werneck (2004), A Hybrid Heuristic for the p-Median Problem; Aiex et al. (2005), GRASP with Path Relinking for Three-Index Assignment; Resende et al. (2010), GRASP and path relinking for the max-min diversity problem; Ribeiro & Resende (2012), Path-relinking intensification methods for stochastic local search algorithms.
algorithms.implementation: Canonical GRASP + reusable local search + quality/diversity elite memory + configurable advanced pairwise path relinking + optional Resende-Werneck generational Evolutionary Path Relinking.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite non-negative integral path distance; nonempty target-directed move set at positive distance; reversible moves; exact optional deltas; finite randomized-RCL objectives; EvPR starts from at least two elites.
algorithms.convergence: Strict integral-distance decrease gives finite pairwise path termination when uncapped; EvPR stops at the first non-improving generation best or its generation cap; no unconditional global-optimum guarantee is claimed.

algorithms.name: Threshold Accepting
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact move-objective evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); O(1) acceptance state beyond the domain trajectory workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Dueck & Scheuer (1990), Threshold accepting: A general purpose optimization algorithm appearing superior to simulated annealing, Journal of Computational Physics 90(1), 161-175
algorithms.implementation: Deterministic sense-aware threshold acceptance over the generic reversible trajectory executor, exact-delta fast path, three built-in monotone threshold schedules and common OptimizationContext lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: Candidate objective values are finite; reversible moves and optional delta evaluations are exact; built-in threshold schedules are non-negative and non-increasing.
algorithms.convergence: Finite termination follows from an active finite generic stopping criterion, neighborhood exhaustion, or a schedule reaching the configured minimum when threshold stopping is enabled. No unconditional finite-time global-optimality guarantee is claimed.

algorithms.name: Great Deluge Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact move-objective evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); O(1) water-level state beyond the domain trajectory workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Dueck (1993), New Optimization Heuristics: The Great Deluge Algorithm and the Record-to-Record Travel, Journal of Computational Physics 104(1), 86-92
algorithms.implementation: Classical absolute water-level acceptance with initial level equal to the initial objective, one positive linear rain-speed parameter, exact-delta reversible execution and accepted-visit best accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Candidate objectives and water levels are finite; rain speed is positive and expressed in objective units; reversible moves and optional exact candidate-objective evaluations are exact.
algorithms.convergence: No unconditional global-optimality guarantee is claimed. Positive linear rain speed progressively tightens the classical boundary; practical termination uses the common stopping contract.

algorithms.name: Record-to-Record Travel
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact move-objective evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); O(1) record-deviation state beyond the domain trajectory workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Dueck (1993), New Optimization Heuristics: The Great Deluge Algorithm and the Record-to-Record Travel, Journal of Computational Physics 104(1), 86-92
algorithms.implementation: Classical fixed absolute deviation around the best accepted record, exact-delta reversible execution and probe-versus-visited best-so-far accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Candidate and record objectives are finite; deviation is non-negative and expressed in objective units; record updates come only from accepted visited states.
algorithms.convergence: With positive fixed deviation RRT may continue inside the record band indefinitely. No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made; termination uses the common stopping contract.

algorithms.name: Late Acceptance Hill Climbing
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) with an exact move-objective evaluator
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + L) for a circular objective-history buffer of length L
algorithms.applicability: Stochastic reversible neighborhoods over any supported representation; exact candidate-objective deltas optional
algorithms.publication: Burke & Bykov (2017), The late acceptance Hill-Climbing heuristic, European Journal of Operational Research 258(1), 70-78
algorithms.implementation: Final Burke-Bykov history-reference acceptance, non-worsening hill-climbing safeguard, monotone-quality circular history, exact-delta fast path and visited-state best accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: History length is positive; candidate objective comparisons are finite; optional exact deltas agree with full evaluation; maximization mirrors the quality ordering.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made. With L=1, acceptance reduces to non-worsening hill climbing; for L>1 the retained history improves monotonically in objective quality.
